en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the *Satpuruṣanirvāṇa*,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Minister Dharma-xian, Grand Master for Illuminating Teaching, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
and Grand Officer of the Third Rank, in accordance with imperial decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Markaṭahradatīrtha Pariveṇa in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Listen attentively now!

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; they are subject to arising and ceasing, lacking solidity and substance. They are not ultimate, they are unreliable, and they are not to be delighted in. You should know this, and you must exert yourselves with diligent effort to seek liberation."
"O Bhikṣus!

Time does not remain long; it shifts and passes from moment to moment. After this period, at the end of the kalpa, the heavens will send no rain and the human world will suffer a parching drought. All the trees and forests, the hundred grains and sprouts, and all the flowers and fruits upon the great earth will wither and dry up, and none shall come to fruition."

"O bhikṣus, you should know that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are subject to arising and ceasing, lacking solidity and substance. They are not ultimate, they are unreliable, and they are not to be delighted in. You should therefore apply yourselves with diligent vigor to seek liberation."
"O Bhikṣus!

At the end of the kalpa, two suns appear and illuminate the world with their heat; as the signs of heat become increasingly intense, all trees and forests upon the great earth—roots, trunks, branches, and leaves—are utterly destroyed and nothing remains."
"Monks! Thus, impermanence cannot be maintained for long; you should now apply yourselves with diligence to swiftly seek liberation.
Furthermore, monks!"

At the end of the kalpa, three suns appear, blazing and illuminating the world. As the intensity of the heat increases beyond measure, it causes the destruction of things to become even more severe; all the small rivers and every spring source upon the great earth are completely exhausted until not even a drop of water remains.
"O bhikṣus, you should know: who is able to escape such impermanence?
Therefore, I now earnestly exhort you to swiftly seek liberation.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus!"

At the end of the kalpa, when the four suns appear and scorch the world, the heat becomes more intense than before; all that exists upon the great earth—the Lake Anavatapta and the four great rivers, the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, the Sītā, and the Vakṣu—all completely dry up and vanish without leaving even a trace of water.
"Monks, you should know: who among those subject to such impermanence can escape it?
Reflect upon this yourselves; do not be indolent, but strive swiftly for liberation.
Furthermore, monks!"

At the end of the kalpa, five suns appear, their blazing heat illuminating the world; as this intense heat prevails, all the waters of the great oceans upon the earth gradually diminish by one hundred yojanas, two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, up to one thousand yojanas.

Since the suns have become so fiercely hot and the rains from heaven have long ceased, the ocean further decreases by two thousand yojanas, three thousand yojanas, and even up to seven thousand yojanas. Once it has diminished in this way, the remaining water in the sea is still seven thousand yojanas deep.
"Furthermore, monks!

In this way, the waters of the great ocean gradually decrease by seven thousand yojanas, then to six thousand yojanas, five thousand yojanas, four thousand yojanas, and so on, until there remain only seven hundred yojanas."
"Furthermore, monks!

In this way, the waters of the great ocean, seven hundred yojanas deep, gradually diminish further until they are six hundred yojanas, five hundred yojanas, four hundred yojanas, and so on, down to seven yojanas."
"Furthermore, monks!
In this way, the water of the great ocean gradually recedes by seven yojanas, then to six yojanas, five yojanas, four yojanas, and so on, until it remains at a depth of seven krośas."
"Furthermore, monks!
In this way, the water of the great ocean gradually diminishes from seven krośas, down to six krośas, five krośas, four krośas, and so on, until there remain only seven tala trees."
"Furthermore, monks!

In this way, the water of the great ocean gradually recedes by the height of seven *tāla* trees, then six *tāla* trees, five *tāla* trees, four *tāla* trees, and so on, until it is only the height of seven men."
"Furthermore, monks!

In this way, the water of the great ocean, measuring seven men in depth, gradually diminishes further to six men, five men, four men, and so on down to one man; it reaches the height of a person's neck, then their ribs, then their navel, then their waist, then their knees, then their ankles, and finally the depth of a single finger, at which point it immediately dries up completely."
"Thereupon, in this world there was only the great earth, mountains, and rivers, and nothing else existed.
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣus!"
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; arising and ceasing without abiding, they are without reality and without solidity.
You should all swiftly seek liberation therein. Furthermore, monks:

At the end of the kalpa, when the six suns appear, the great earth becomes intensely hot and the mountains and rocks melt away; even from Sumeru, the King of Mountains, a slight smoke arises, just as black smoke rises from a kiln burning tiles.
"Therefore, O Bhikṣus, this world is incapable of being scrutinized.
Thus, impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing, and lacking stability, you should apply yourselves with diligent vigor, abandon the heart of craving and attachment, and swiftly seek liberation."
"Furthermore, monks!

At the end of the kalpa, seven suns appear; their heat becomes extreme and suddenly fire breaks out, like burning ten bundles of wood, then a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, and hundreds of thousands of millions of bundles, until even the small chiliocosm and the various heavens of the six desire realms become a single mass of fire."

Having burned the desire realm, the fire of the first dhyāna in the Brahma-world also spontaneously arises, incinerating all the palaces of the receptacle world—some a hundred yojanas high, some two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, and so on up to seven thousand yojanas—so that these palaces all become masses of flame.
In the neighboring realm of the Second Dhyāna, there were newly born Brahmakāyika devas who, seeing the flames from below, were struck with great terror and sought to escape the calamity of fire.
At that time, the elder devas of the Second Dhyāna said to them:
"You have been born in my palace due to your past merit; simply settle your minds and do not give way to fear, for the fires of this lower realm will soon be extinguished."
Having spoken thus, suddenly a great wind arose and blew away the smoke and flames; even the ashes and embers were entirely gone.

It was as if someone were to light a lamp with ghee in the midst of empty space: once the flame is extinguished, not even a trace of black smoke or ash remains; the extinction of that fire was likewise so.
The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus!

Conditioned phenomena arise and perish without abiding; they are inverted dharmas, lacking solidity and lacking reality. They are not ultimate and are not to be delighted in. Therefore, distance yourselves from craving and attachment, and swiftly seek liberation."
"If there is no craving or attachment, by what cause and by what condition do the great earth and all the devas perish and cease to appear?
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!

In the past, there appeared a Buddha named Lokeśvararāja (The King of the World), who was the Tathāgata Sunetra (Wondrous Eye). He had an immeasurable and boundless assembly of śrāvakas, as well as an assembly of Brahmā devas and non-Buddhist practitioners who were free from desire and possessed of supernatural powers."
That Tathāgata Subhacakṣus taught for the sake of his śrāvakas the Dharma of the profound, definitive, and pure Brahma-faring.

At that time, the bhikṣus attained perfection in all the rules of discipline and practiced according to their inclinations: some cultivated the four immeasurable meditations (*apramāṇa*) and, severing the defilements of the lower realms of desire, were reborn in the Brahma-world;

others, according to their inclinations, desired to be reborn in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmitavaśavartin*), the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*nirmāṇarati*), Tuṣita Heaven, Yāma Heaven, Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, or the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājika*); others desired to be reborn in the families of kṣatriyas, brahmins, or among householders and elders.
At that time, the Tathāgata Sunetra had this thought:
"I shall now cause that assembly of śrāvakas to act together, be born together, and possess equal power, so that they may enter the second dhyāna of Maitreya."
Having reflected thus, he immediately entered the second dhyāna of Maitreya.
At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of śrāvakas and non-Buddhists all practiced that same meditative concentration and were reborn together above in the Brahma Heaven.
The Buddha said, “Monks!
That Tathāgata Sunetra of the past was not some other Buddha; he was none other than myself.”

Although those multitudes have been born in the Second Dhyāna and thus escaped the calamity of the fires below, they have not yet abandoned the seeds of greed, hatred, and delusion, and are therefore unable to be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"O Bhikṣus!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is the Teacher of gods and humans; he is far removed from all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, and is liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress. Furthermore, for the sake of the Brahmās, the Śrāvakas, and the assembly, he proclaims the pure practice of the Dharma according to their needs."
Having each heard this, some completely severed their conceptual discriminations along with the innate afflictions and realized the fruit of *anāgāmin*;
some completely severed their conceptual discriminations along with six grades of innate afflictions and realized the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*;

and some, although they had exhausted their conceptual discriminations but not yet severed the innate afflictions, realized the fruit of *srotāpanna*, and after experiencing seven rebirths among devas and humans, became *arhats*.
The Buddha said,
“Bhikṣus! By such renunciation,
such holy life, and such realization of the fruit, one attains the end of suffering and achieves liberation.”
"Now, with this resolve, abandon craving and attachment, and set out upon the path to awakening.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these teachings, that bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha said, was filled with great joy; he accepted it with faith and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Samantabhadrotsāhana Spoken by the Buddha.
